text: a(n) = ((n^2+(4+i)*n+4+4*i)/8)*(1+i)^n + ((n^2+(4-i)*n+4-4*i)/8)*(1-i)^n, from which the conjectures above follow (see Fried link). - _Sela Fried_, Jan 28 2026
author: Sela Fried

name: Maximum number of distinct folds after folding a square sheet of paper n times.
text: Conjecture: a(n) = 2*a(n-1) + 4 - n, for n > 2.

name: Triangle read by rows: T(n,k) is the maximum number of connected endofunctions that are spanning subgraphs of a semi-regular loopless digraph on n vertices each with out-degree k.
text: Conjecture: T(n,n-2) = A000435(n-1)*(n-2) for n > 2. From _Andrew Howroyd_, Jan 08 2023: (Start)
author: Andrew Howroyd

name: a(n) = Sum_{k=0..n} binomial(n,k) * binomial(4*k,k).
author: R. J. Mathar

name: a(1) = 1; for n > 1, a(n) is the smallest positive number which has not appeared that shares a factor with the sum of the first n terms of the Champernowne string starting from 1.
text: For the Champernowne string starting from 1 see A033307. In the first 100000 terms there are 45 fixed points: 1, 4, 5, 6, 7, ..., 252, 264, 319. It is plausible no more exist. The sequence is conjectured to be a permutation of the positive integers.

name: Prime Maze Room 11, opposite parity of A059459 starting from prime room 11.
text: Conjecture: Room 2 and Room 11 are unlinked, i.e., two separate mazes or branches/trees, as they are of opposite parities.

name: Triangle read by rows. Each term of the triangle is positive and distinct. In row k are the next k least numbers such that the sum of any one number from each of the first k rows is a prime number.
text: Defining this same triangle from another angle, e.g., by discovering and describing a regularity in its structure, and/or proving its infinitude, is equivalent to proving the twin prime conjecture. An independent proof of the latter may not prove the infiniteness of this sequence, however.

name: Lexicographically earliest sequence of distinct nonnegative integers such that the sequence A051699(a(n)) (distance from the nearest prime) has the same sequence of digits.
text: Conjectured to be a permutation of the nonnegative integers. The inverse permutation would start (3, 0, 2, 4, 9, 39, 10, 48, 20, 6, 1, 58, 21, 75, 25, 14, ...).

name: Lexicographically earliest sequence of distinct nonnegative integers such that the sequence d(n) = dist(a(n), SQUARES) has the same sequence of digits.
text: Conjectured to be a permutation of the nonnegative integers. The inverse permutation would start (0, 2, 3, 11, 9, 12, 4, 7, 19, 21, 1, 8, 16, 20, 18, 24, ...)

name: Lexicographically earliest sequence of distinct nonnegative integers such that the sequence d(n) = A296239(a(n)) has the same sequence of digits, where A296239 gives the distance from the nearest Fibonacci number, cf. A000045.
text: Conjectured to be a permutation of the nonnegative integers. The inverse permutation would start (0, 4, 25, 37, 3, 54, 6, 7, 104, 12, 2, 13, 1, 106, 20, ...).

name: Maximal number of moves needed by a knight to reach every cell from a fixed position on an n X n X n chessboard, or -1 if it is not possible to reach every square.
text: The author conjectures that, for any n greater than 3, a(n) = n, while all the 10 independent cases has been manually checked for n = 5 and n = 6 (if n = 4, there are only 4 cases to be checked in order to show that a(4) = 4). As noted by Eric Weisstein in A232007, a(n) is the graph diameter of the n X n X n knight graph (or -1 if the graph is disconnected). In general, by assuming n > 3, it is not hard to prove that d(n,k)(N), the knight graph diameter for a k-dimensional n X n X ... X n board, belongs to the closed interval [(ceiling(n*sqrt(k))/sqrt(5), k*n] if n is odd and to [(ceiling(n*sqrt(k))/sqrt(5), k*(n + 1)] if n is even. From _Pontus von Brömssen_, Jan 13 2023: (Start)
author: Pontus von Brömssen

name: Maximal number of moves needed by a knight to reach every cell from a fixed position on an n X n X n chessboard, or -1 if it is not possible to reach every square.
text: a(n) = n for n >= 4 (conjectured by author; proved above).

name: Dirichlet inverse of function f(n) = 1 + A048675(n), where A048675(n) is fully additive with a(p) = 2^(1-PrimePi(p)).
text: Conjecture: the only odd term that occurs more than once is 1 = a(1) = a(4).

name: a(1) = 1, a(2) = 3; for n > 2, a(n) is the smallest positive number which has not appeared that shares a factor with |a(n-1) - a(n-2)| while the difference |a(n) - a(n-1)| is distinct from all previous differences |a(i) - a(i-1)|, i=2..n-1.
text: In the first 100000 terms the only fixed point is a(1) = 1; it is unknown if more exist. The sequence is conjectured to be a permutation of the positive integers.

name: a(1) = 1, a(2) = 2; thereafter let p be the smallest prime that does not divide a(n-2)*a(n-1), then a(n) is the smallest multiple of p that is not yet in the sequence.
text: Conjecture: The primes appear in their natural order.

name: a(1) = 0; thereafter a(n) is the largest a(i) + i which is < n among i = 1..n-1.
text: Conjectured run lengths are A272729, and the terms which occur here are partial sums of A272729.

name: Parity of A353418, where A353418 is Dirichlet inverse of the characteristic function for numbers k where A156552(k) is a multiple of 3.
text: a(n) <= A353269(n). [Conjectured. Note that as A329609 is not a multiplicative semigroup, the proof cannot be similar to that given in A353348 for A359826. See also A359835]

name: a(n) = Sum_{k=0..n} binomial(n*k,n+k).
text: Conjectures: a(2^k) == 0 (mod 2^(k-1)) and a(3^k) == 0 (mod 3^(k+2)) for k >= 2; a(p^k) == 0 (mod p^(k+1)) for all primes p >= 5.

name: a(0) = 0; for n > 0, a(n) is the smallest positive number not occurring earlier such that the ones' complement of the binary string of a(n-1) + a(n) does not appear in the binary string concatenation of a(0)..a(n-1).
text: In the first 100000 terms the fixed points are 55, 123, 1779, 2009, although it is likely more exist. The sequence is conjectured to be a permutation of the positive integers. Note that 1 does not appear until the 160th term.

name: Number of vertices among all distinct circles that can be constructed from a 2 x n square grid of points using only a compass.
text: A circle is constructed for every pair of the 2 x n points, the first point defines the circle's center while the second the radius distance. The number of distinct circles constructed from the 2 x n points is conjectured to be 4*A001859(n-1).

name: a(n) is the smallest prime q such that A305411(n) + q is a square.
text: A305411 is conjectured to have only 103 terms.

name: a(n) = coefficient of x^n in A(x) such that 2 = Sum_{n=-oo..+oo} (-1)^n * x^(n*(3*n-1)/2) * A(x)^(3*n) * (1 + x^n*A(x)).
text: Conjecture: a(n)/2 == A000041(n) (mod 2) for n >= 1; that is, a(n) is even, and a(n)/2 has the same parity as the number of partitions of n, for n >= 1. Conjecture: a(n) == A361552(n+1) (mod 4) for n >= 0. - _Paul D. Hanna_, Mar 19 2023
author: Paul D. Hanna

name: a(n) = coefficient of x^n in A(x) such that 2 = Sum_{n=-oo..+oo} (-1)^n * x^(n*(3*n-1)/2) * A(x)^(3*n) * (1 + x^n*A(x)).
text: Conjecture: a(n) == A361552(n+1) (mod 4) for n >= 0. - _Paul D. Hanna_, Mar 19 2023
author: Paul D. Hanna

name: The number of practical numbers strictly between A005153(n) and A005153(n)^(1+1/n).
text: This sequence is based on Sun's conjecture that A005153(n)^(1/n) is a strictly decreasing sequence for n >= 3. This conjecture states for practical numbers what Firoozbakht's conjecture says for prime numbers, and implies that a(n) > 0 for n >= 3. It is valid at least for n <= 9991. The corresponding sequence for primes is A182134.

name: Largest k < n such that n! / k! = m! = A000142(m) for some m.
text: Surányi conjectured (cf. Erdős and Habsieger references and A003135) that a(10) = 7 corresponding to 10! = 7! * 6! is the only nontrivial solution, i.e., other than a(n) = n-1 for n = m! and a(n) = 1 otherwise.

name: Number of non-crossing antichain covers of {1,...,n} without singletons.
author: R. J. Mathar

name: Number of vertices in a Farey fan of order n.
text: The number of vertices along each edge is A005728(n), while the number of regions is conjectured to equal A005598(n) = 1 + Sum_{i=1..n} (n-i+1)*phi(i). The regions count the number of distinct approximate representations of straight lines y = mx + b that can be drawn on an x-y integer raster, where x, y, and b are restricted to [0,n) and 0 <= m <=1.

name: Primes p such that each prime < p in the prime factorization of 2^(p-1) - 1 has exponent 1.
text: Conjecture: 2^(a(n)-1) - 1 is always squarefree.

name: Number of integer partitions of n such that the parts have the same mean as the multiplicities.
text: Conjecture: If n is squarefree, then a(n) = 0.

name: Numbers for which there exists an integer partition such that the parts have the same mean as the multiplicities.
text: Conjecture: No term > 1 is squarefree.

name: Numbers k such that sigma_2(k^2 + 1) == 0 (mod k).
text: Conjecture: the sequence contains infinitely many Fibonacci numbers (see A360107).

name: a(n) = 1 if there are no prime factors p of n for which the 2-adic valuation of p-1 is less than that of n-1, otherwise 0.
text: a(n) = [A333570(n) <= 2] = [A360112(n) <= 2]. (Conjectured by Sequence Machine) - _Antti Karttunen_, May 14 2025
author: Antti Karttunen

name: Triangle read by rows where row n is the largest (or middle or n-th) column of the reverse pyramid summation of order n described in A359087.
text: T(n,k) = 3^(k-1)*n - 2*A132894(k-1) for 1 <= k <= n (conjectured).

name: Primitive prime powers. p is a primitive prime power iff it is an odd prime power that exceeds the preceding odd prime power by more than any smaller odd prime power does. ('Prime power' defined in the sense of A246655.)
text: Conjecture: Primitive prime powers are primes.

name: Lexicographically earliest infinite sequence of distinct positive numbers such that, for n > 2, a(n) shares a factor with a(n-2) + a(n-1) but shares no factor with a(n-2).
text: In the first 100000 terms the fixed points for n > 2 are 3, 6, 441, 1677, 3629, 9701, 17131, although it is likely more exist. The sequence is conjectured to be a permutation of the positive integers.

name: Number of integer partitions of n with more adjacent equal parts than distinct parts.
text: Conjecture: a(n) ~ A000041(n). - _Vaclav Kotesovec_, Nov 20 2026
author: Vaclav Kotesovec

name: Determinant of the matrix [L(j+k) + d(j,k)]_{1<=j, k<=n}, where L(n) denotes the Lucas number A000032(n), and d(j,k) is 1 or 0 according as j = k or not.
text: Conjecture 1: Let v(0) = 2, v(1) = A, and v(n+1) = A*v(n) + v(n-1) for n > 0. Then A^2*det[v(j+k) + d(j,k)]_{1<=j, k<=n} = v(n+1)^2 - (A^2 + 4)*(n mod 2) for any positive integer n. In particular, a(n) = L(n+1)^2 - 5*(n mod 2) for all n > 0.

name: Determinant of the matrix [L(j+k) + d(j,k)]_{1<=j, k<=n}, where L(n) denotes the Lucas number A000032(n), and d(j,k) is 1 or 0 according as j = k or not.
text: Conjecture 2: Let v(0) = 2, v(1) = A, and v(n+1) = A*v(n) - v(n-1) for n > 0. Then det[v(j+k) + d(j,k)]_{1<=j, k<=n} = u(n+1)^2 - n^2 for any positive integer n, where u(0) = 0, u(1) = 1, and u(n+1) = A*u(n) - u(n-1) for all n > 0.

name: Determinant of the matrix [L(j+k) + d(j,k)]_{1<=j, k<=n}, where L(n) denotes the Lucas number A000032(n), and d(j,k) is 1 or 0 according as j = k or not.
text: Conjecture 3: Let F(n) denote the Fibonacci number A000045(n). Then, for any positive integer n, we have det[F(j+k) + d(j,k)]_{1<=j, k<=n} = F(n+1)^2 + (n mod 2).

name: Indices of the nonprimitive rows of the Wythoff array (A035513); see Comments.
text: In a row of the Wythoff array, either every two consecutive terms are relatively prime or else no two consecutive terms are relatively prime. In the first case, we call the row primitive, as in A332938. Otherwise, the row is an integer multiple of a tail of a preceding row, and we call the row nonprimitive.  Conjecture: the limiting proportion of nonprimitive rows exists and is approximately 0.392.

name: a(n) = number of the row of the Wythoff array (A035513) that includes prime(n).
text: Conjecture: every primitive row number, as defined in A332938, occurs infinitely many times in this sequence.

name: a(n) = number of the column of the Wythoff array (A035513) that includes prime(n).
text: Conjecture: every positive integer occurs infinitely many times in this sequence.

name: a(n) = number of the antidiagonal of the Wythoff array (A035513) that includes prime(n).
text: Conjecture: Only a finite number of positive integers are missing.

name: a(n) = number of the diagonal of the Wythoff array, A035513, that includes prime(n). See Comments.
text: The indexing of diagonals is given in A191360. Conjecture: every integer occurs infinitely many times in this sequence; i.e., every diagonal includes infinitely many primes.

name: Numbers k such that, in a listing of all congruence classes of positive integers, the k-th congruence class contains k. Here the class r mod m (with r in {1,...,m}) precedes the class a' mod b' (with r' in {1,...,m'}) iff m < m' or r > r'.
text: Above conjecture confirmed with more terms and linear recurrence.  See supporting formula below. - _Ray Chandler_, Feb 10 2025
author: Ray Chandler

name: Indices of records in A018804.
text: Conjecture: a(n) ~ exp(4*(n-1)/21). - _Matthew Russell Downey_, Jul 25 2023
author: Matthew Russell Downey

name: Let C consist of 1 together with all numbers with at least two distinct prime factors; this is the lexicographically earliest infinite sequence {a(n)} of distinct elements of C such that, for n>2, a(n) has a common factor with a(n-1) but not with a(n-2).
text: Conjecture: The sequence is a permutation of C.

name: a(0) = 0; for n > 0, a(n) is the smallest positive number not occurring earlier such that neither the binary string a(n-1) + a(n) nor the same string reversed appear in the binary string concatenation of a(0)..a(n-1).
text: As in A357082 the main concentration of terms is along the line a(n) = n, so there are numerous fixed points - there are 24 fixed points in the first 200000 terms. The sequence is conjectured to be a permutation of the positive integers.

name: a(n) = index of the diagonal of the natural number array, A000027, that includes prime(n). See Comments.
text: The indexing of diagonals is given in A191360. Conjecture: Every odd-indexed diagonal contains infinitely many primes.

name: a(n) is the least prime p not already in the sequence such that a(n-1) + p is a triprime; a(1) = 2.
text: Conjecture: every prime eventually appears in the sequence.

name: Expansion of g.f. A(x) satisfying A(x) = Series_Reversion( x - x*A'(x)*A(x) ).
text: a(n) ~ c * n! * n^alfa / LambertW(1)^n, where alfa = 1.5447806483693... and c = 0.02888888614196289496..., conjecture: alfa = 2*(2*LambertW(1) - 1 + 1/(1 + LambertW(1))). - _Vaclav Kotesovec_, Feb 22 2023
author: Vaclav Kotesovec

name: Expansion of A(x) satisfying [x^n] A(x)^n / (1 + x*A(x)^n)^n = 0 for n > 0.
text: Conjecture: alpha = 3*LambertW(1) - 2 + 1/(1 + LambertW(1)) = 0.33953361459446... (End)

name: a(n) is the least positive integer k such that k*(k+1)*...*(k+n-1) does not contain the digit 2, or -1 if there is no such k.
text: Conjecture: a(n) = -1 for n = 31 and all n >= 33.

name: Numbers k that set records in A355432.
text: Conjecture: for n > 2, subset of A364702. - _Michael De Vlieger_, Oct 04 2024
author: Michael De Vlieger

name: Largest k such that the decimal representation of 2^k is missing any n-digit string.
text: All terms are conjectural, checked up to 10^6.

name: Square array A(n, k), n, k > 0, read by antidiagonals upwards; A(n, k) = A360613(2*n-1) * A360613(2*k).
text: Conjecture: all integers appear in this sequence.

name: a(n) is the smallest nonnegative integer that satisfies p(a(n)+1) - p(a(n)) >= n, where p denotes the number partition function.
text: Conjecture: except for the values 2, 4 and 6, this sequence includes all the nonnegative integers.

name: Number triangle T associated with 2-Stirling numbers and Lehmer-Comtet numbers (see Comments and Formula section).
text: Conjecture: the transpose of this array is the upper triangular matrix U in the LU factorization of the array of Stirling numbers of the second kind read as a square array; the corresponding lower triangular array L is the triangle of Stirling numbers of the second kind. See the example section below. - _Peter Bala_, Oct 10 2023
author: Peter Bala

name: Number triangle T associated with 2-Stirling numbers and Lehmer-Comtet numbers (see Comments and Formula section).
text: All conjectures in the formula section and the one by Bala are true (see Fried link). Notice that U in the LU factorization is not the transpose of T, but rather obtained from T. - _Sela Fried_, Aug 18 2026
author: Sela Fried

name: Number triangle T associated with 2-Stirling numbers and Lehmer-Comtet numbers (see Comments and Formula section).
text: Conjectured formulas:

name: a(n) is the minimum sum of a completely multiplicative sign sequence of length n.
text: Conjecture: For every n >= 22 there exists completely multiplicative sign sequence of length n with the minimal sum, which have +1's on initial primes and -1's on the remaining primes, i.e., its subsequence on primes is ++...+--...- for some number of +1's. First differences are either 1 or -1. This is because optimum sequences for n cannot have a sum less than one less than those for n-1 and similarly optimum sequences for n cannot have a sum greater than one more than those for n-1. A zero difference is not possible because terms alternate between even and odd. - _Andrew Howroyd_, Feb 16 2023
author: Andrew Howroyd

name: a(n) is the minimum sum of a completely multiplicative sign sequence of length n.
text: Conjecture: a(n) < A002819(n) for n > 20. |a(n) - a(n-1)| = 1 for n > 0. - _Andrew Howroyd_, Feb 16 2023
author: Andrew Howroyd

name: Matrix inverse of A360657.
text: Conjectured formulas: 1. Matrix product of A354794 and T without column 0 equals A215534. 2. Matrix product of T and A354794 without column 0 equals A132013. 3. E.g.f. of column k > 0: Sum_{n >= k} T(n, k) * t^(n-1) / (n-1)! = (1 - t) * (Sum_{n >= k} A354795(n, k) * t^(n-1) / (n-1)!). All three conjectures are true (see Fried link in A360657). - _Sela Fried_, Aug 18 2026
author: Sela Fried

name: Matrix inverse of A360657.
text: All three conjectures are true (see Fried link in A360657). - _Sela Fried_, Aug 18 2026
author: Sela Fried

name: Decimal expansion of Sum_{m>=1} 1/(1/4 + z(m)^2) where z(m) is the imaginary part of the m-th nontrivial zero of the Dirichlet beta function whose real part is 1/2.
text: Conjecture: Nontrivial zeros whose real part is not 1/2 do not exist.

name: Number of primes of the form k^2+1 between n^2 and 2*n^2 exclusive.
text: Conjecture: Except for n = 7, between the square of an integer n > 1 and the double of its square there is always at least one prime number of the form k^2+1.

name: Numbers whose squares have at most 2 digits less than 8.
text: Conjecture: Sequence has 72 terms, with largest term 940206833.

name: Array read by antidiagonals: T(m,n) is the number of vertices in the longest induced path in the grid graph P_m X P_n.
text: T(4,n) = A047408(n+1) - [n = 4] (conjectured), with Iverson bracket [.] = 1 if true, 0 else. (End) T(4,n) = 8*n/3 + (n mod 3)/3 + 1 if (n mod 3) \in {0,1}, 8*n/3 + (n mod 3)/3 if (n mod 3) = 2, 11 if n = 4. - _Alain Goupil_, Jul 20 2026
author: Alain Goupil

name: Maximum number of vertices in an induced tree in the n X n grid graph.
text: Conjecture: a(n) = n^2 - A354673(n). - _Andrew Howroyd_, Jul 25 2026
author: Andrew Howroyd

name: Table T(i,j), i >= 0, j >= 0, read by antidiagonals giving the smallest number of moves needed to win Integer Lunar Lander, starting from position (i,j). Game rules in comments.
text: Conjecture 1: For all i, j, T(i,j) differs from its eight neighbors by at most 3. The array of differences {T(i+1,j) - T(i,j)} might be worth studying, as well as the array {T(i,j) mod 2}. - _N. J. A. Sloane_, Feb 25 2023
author: N. J. A. Sloane

name: Table T(i,j), i >= 0, j >= 0, read by antidiagonals giving the smallest number of moves needed to win Integer Lunar Lander, starting from position (i,j). Game rules in comments.
text: Conjecture 2 (Start) The zeroth row (0,j) is T(0,j) = 1+ floor(sqrt(4j-3)). j>0. Let t_k = k(k+1)/2 be a triangular number. Then the i-th row, {(i,j), j>=0}, is given by   T(i,j) = T(0, j+t_{i-1}) + i for i>0. In other words, to get the i-th row, shift the zeroth row to the left by i*(i-1)/2 places and add i to each term. This would imply that the leading column, T(i,0), is equal to i+1+floor(sqrt(2*i^2-2*i-3)) for i >= 2. (End) - _N. J. A. Sloane_, Feb 25 2023
author: N. J. A. Sloane

name: Table T(i,j), i >= 0, j >= 0, read by antidiagonals giving the smallest number of moves needed to win Integer Lunar Lander, starting from position (i,j). Game rules in comments.
text: Conjecture 1 seems to hold for all (i,j) except (1,0) and (2,1). - _M. F. Hasler_, Feb 27 2023
author: M. F. Hasler

name: Smallest number of moves needed to win Integer Lunar Lander from starting position (n,0).
text: Conjecture: For n >= 2, a(n) =  n+1+floor(sqrt(2*n^2-2*n-3)). - _N. J. A. Sloane_, Feb 26 2023
author: N. J. A. Sloane

name: Smallest number of moves needed to win Integer Lunar Lander with a starting position of (n,n).
text: The conjectured formula for A360923 implies a formula for a(n). - _N. J. A. Sloane_, Feb 26 2023
author: N. J. A. Sloane

name: Odd numbers which cannot be expressed as p + q*(q+1) where p and q are primes.
text: It is conjectured that 1446377 is the largest term.

name: Odd numbers which cannot be expressed as p + q*(q+1) where p and q are primes.
text: The expression p + q*(q+1) resembles the expression p + 2*q used in Lemoine's conjecture.

name: Odd numbers which cannot be expressed as p + q*(q-1) where p and q are primes.
text: It is conjectured that 772277 is the largest odd integer which cannot be expressed as p + q*(q-1) where p and q are primes.

name: Odd numbers which cannot be expressed as p + q*(q-1) where p and q are primes.
text: The expression p + q*(q-1) resembles the expression p + 2*q used in Lemoine's conjecture.

name: a(1) = 2, a(2) = 3; for n > 2, a(n) is the smallest number greater than 1 that has not appeared such that |a(n) - a(n-1)| has a common factor with a(n-2).
text: In the first 100000 terms the fixed points are 10, 16, 42, 52, 66; it is likely no more exist. The sequence is conjectured to be a permutation of the positive integers > 1.

name: G.f. A(x) satisfies: 1 = Sum_{n>=0} (-x/2)^n * (A(x)^n + (-1)^n)^n.
text: Conjecture: a(0) = 1, a(2*A161674(k) + 1) == 2 (mod 4) for k >= 1, otherwise a(n) == 0 (mod 4). A161674 lists positions n such that A010060(n) + A010060(n+2) = 1, where A010060 is the Thue-Morse sequence.

name: a(n) = 3*(4*n)!/(n!*(n+1)!^3).
text: Conjecture: a(n) is odd iff n = 2^k - 1 for some k >= 0.

name: a(n) = 2520*(4*n)!/(n!*(n+2)!^3).
text: Conjecture: a(n) is odd iff n = 2^k - 2 for some k >= 1.

name: a(n) = 9979200 * (4*n)!/(n!*(n+3)!^3).
text: Conjecture: a(n) is odd iff n = 2^k - 3 for some k >= 2.

name: a(n) = n! * [x^n] (1 + x)^n * exp(x*(1 + x)^n).
text: We conjecture that a(n+k) == a(n) (mod k) for all n and k. If true, then for each k, the sequence a(n) taken modulo k is a periodic sequence and the period divides k. For example, modulo 7 the sequence becomes [1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 0, 4, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 0, 4, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 0, 4, ...], apparently a periodic sequence of period 7. More generally, let F(x) and G(x) denote power series with integer coefficients with F(0) = G(0) = 1. Define b(n) = n! * [x^n] exp(x*G(x)^n)*F(x)^n. Then we conjecture that b(n+k) == b(n) (mod k) for all n and k. The conjectures above are true, see Turazashvili links. - _Nikoloz Turazashvili_, Aug 22 2026
author: Nikoloz Turazashvili

name: a(n) = n! * [x^n] (1 + x)^n * exp(x*(1 + x)^n).
text: More generally, let F(x) and G(x) denote power series with integer coefficients with F(0) = G(0) = 1. Define b(n) = n! * [x^n] exp(x*G(x)^n)*F(x)^n. Then we conjecture that b(n+k) == b(n) (mod k) for all n and k. The conjectures above are true, see Turazashvili links. - _Nikoloz Turazashvili_, Aug 22 2026
author: Nikoloz Turazashvili

name: a(n) = n! * [x^n] (1 + x)^n * exp(x*(1 + x)^n).
text: The conjectures above are true, see Turazashvili links. - _Nikoloz Turazashvili_, Aug 22 2026
author: Nikoloz Turazashvili

name: Expansion of g.f. A(x) satisfying A(x) = Series_Reversion(x - x^3*A'(x)^2).
text: Conjecture: a(n) == 1 (mod 3) iff n = (3^k - 1)/2 for k >= 0, otherwise a(n) == 0 (mod 3).

name: Sum of the j-th number with binary weight n-j+1 over all j in [n].
text: Conjecture: a(n) ~ 19 * 2^n / 6. - _Vaclav Kotesovec_, Mar 04 2023
author: Vaclav Kotesovec

name: a(n) = largest sqrt(2*n)-smooth divisor of binomial(2*n, n).
text: Binomial(2*n, n)/a(n) and A263931(n)/a(n) are coprime with a(n) and squarefree. By the Erdős squarefree conjecture, proved in 1996, no a(n) with n >= 5 is squarefree.

name: Maximum squared inverse distance from the origin to the hyperplane defined by hypercube points.
text: Because it is not known if the squared inverse distances are always integers, this is a sequence of numerators (and the known corresponding denominators are all 1). The next two terms are conjectured to be 59 and 203 (distinct from sequences already in the OEIS).

name: a(n) = k such that A360519(k) = A361102(n), or -1 if A361102(n) never appears in A360519.
text: Conjectured to be a permutation of the natural numbers (and if so, -1 will never appear). See A361104 for the putative inverse permutation.

name: Let p = n-th odd prime; a(n) = index where 2*p appears in A360519, or -1 if 2*p never appears.
text: It is conjectured that every 2*prime(n) (n>1) appears in A360519. A proof of this would be a big step towards proving that every term of C appears in A360519.

name: Let b = A360519; let Lg = gcd(b(n-1),b(n)), Rg = gcd(b(n),b(n+1)); let L(n) = prod_{primes p|Lg} p-part of b(n), R(n) = prod_{primes p|Rg} p-part of b(n), M(n) = b(n)/(L(n)*R(n)); sequence gives M(n).
text: Conjecture: All terms are odd, and every odd number eventually appears.

name: Multiplicative with a(p^e) = e^4, p prime and e > 0.
text: Conjecture: log(log(c(k)))/k converges to a constant (around 0.315).

name: a(n) = n for n <= 3. Let h, i, j represent a(n-3), a(n-2), a(n-1) respectively. For n > 3, if there is a symmetric difference in the sets of distinct primes dividing h and j, with greatest member p then a(n) is the least novel multiple of p. Otherwise, a(n) is the least novel k such that (k,i) > 1.
text: Conjectured to be a permutation of the natural numbers, with primes in natural order.

name: a(n) = phi(n)^4.
text: Conjecture: c(k)*log(k) converges to a constant (around 0.534).

name: Number of 4n-step lattice paths starting and ending at (0,0) that do not go above the diagonal x=y or below the x-axis using steps in {(1,1), (1,-1), (-1,0)}.
text: Conjecture: alpha = 1 + Pi/arctan(sqrt(2)) = 1 + Pi/A195696. (End)

name: a(n) is the number of equations in the set {x^2 + 2y^2 = n, 2x^2 + 3y^2 = n, ..., k*x^2 + (k+1)*y^2 = n, ..., n*x^2 + (n+1)*y^2 = n} which admit at least one nonnegative integer solution.
text: Conjecture: a(n) = 2 for infinitely many n.

name: a(n) = n! * Sum_{k=0..n} binomial(n*k,n-k)/k!.
text: It appears that a(n) == 1 (mod 4) and a(5*n+2) == 0 (mod 5) for all n. More generally we conjecture that a(n+k) == a(n) (mod k) for all n and k. If true, then for each k, the sequence a(n) taken modulo k is a periodic sequence and the period divides k.

name: a(n) = n! * Sum_{k=0..n} binomial(n*k,n-k)/k!.
text: Let F(x) and G(x) be power series with integer coefficients with G(0) = 1. Define b(n) = n! * [x^n] F(x)*exp(x*G(x)^n). Then we conjecture that b(n+k) == b(n) (mod k) for all n and k. The present sequence is the case F(x) = 1, G(x) = 1 + x. Cf. A278070. (End)

name: For the odd numbers 2n + 1, the least practical number r such that 2n + 1 = r + p where p is prime.
text: Conjecture by _Hal M. Switkay_: every odd number, beginning with 3, is the sum of a prime number and a practical number. Note that this conjecture occupies the space between the unproven Goldbach conjecture and the theorem that every even number, beginning with 2, is the sum of two practical numbers (Melfi's 1996 proof of Margenstern's conjecture).

name: For the odd number 2n + 1, the least primitive practical number r such that 2n + 1 = r + p where p is prime.
text: Conjecture: every odd number, beginning with 3, is the sum of a prime number and a primitive practical number. This is a tighter conjecture than that posed by _Hal M. Switkay_ (see comments of A005153).

name: a(1) = 1, a(2) = 2; for n > 2, a(n) is the smallest positive number which has not appeared that shares a factor with a(n-2) + a(n-1) while the sum a(n) + a(n-1) is distinct from all previous sums a(i) + a(i-1), i=2..n-1.
text: In the first 100000 terms the fixed points are 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 39, 91, 112; it is likely no more exist. The sequence is conjectured to be a permutation of the positive integers.

name: Lexicographically earliest infinite sequence of distinct elements of A000469 such that, for n > 2, a(n) has a common factor with a(n-1) but not with a(n-2).
text: Conjecture: The sequence is a permutation of A000469.

name: The binary expansion of a(n) specifies which primes divide A361321(n).
text: Conjecture: The sequence is a permutation of A057716.

name: a(n) = k such that A000469(k) =  A361321(n).
text: Conjectured to be a permutation of the natural numbers (if not then there exists a k such that A000469(k) does not appear in A361321).

name: a(n) = k such that A361321(k) = A000469(n), or -1 if A000469(n) never appears in A361321.
text: Conjectured to be a permutation of the natural numbers (and if so, -1 will never appear).

name: Numbers that reach 0 after a suitable series of split-and-multiply operations (see Comments for precise definition).
text: a(2894 + k) = 3112 + k for all k >= 0 (conjectured). - _M. F. Hasler_, Apr 05 2023
author: M. F. Hasler

name: Multiplicative with a(p^e) = e - 1.
text: Conjecture: a(n) = abs(A298826(n)). a(n) > 0 if and only if n is powerful (A001694). - _Amiram Eldar_, Aug 15 2023
author: Amiram Eldar

name: a(n) = 1 if A135504(n+1) = 2 * A135504(n), otherwise 0.
text: a(n) = 1 if A135506(n) is not prime, otherwise 0. [Conjectured]

name: Numbers k such that x(k+1) = 2 * x(k), when x(1)=1 and x(n) = x(n-1) + lcm(x(n-1),n), i.e., x(n) = A135504(n).
text: It is conjectured that this sequence gives also all numbers k for which A135506(k) is not a prime. See Ruiz-Cabello paper.

name: a(n) = bigomega(A249670(A003961(n))).
text: Conjecture: There are no 1's in this sequence. If true, it would imply that there are no odd terms in A065997.

name: Index of n in A359804, or -1 if n never appears there.
text: Conjectured to be a permutation of the natural numbers.

name: a(1) = 1. Thereafter if a(n-1) is a novel term, a(n) = d(a(n-1)); otherwise, if a(n-1) is the t-th non-novel term, a(n) = a(n-1) + d(a(t)), where d is the divisor function A000005.
text: It is an obvious conjecture that every number eventually appears, but is there a proof?

name: Novel terms in A361511, in order of appearance.
text: By definition the terms are distinct. It is an obvious conjecture that every number eventually appears, but is there a proof?

name: a(n) = index of first appearance of n in A361511, or -1 if n never appears.
text: Conjecture: This is a permutation of the positive integers.

name: Let h,i,j be the latest 3 terms in the sequence, starting with a(1)=1, a(2)=2, a(3)=3. Let R = rad(h*i*j), where rad is A007947, and let S be the smallest number of terms in U = {h,i,j} which are divisible by any prime p dividing R. Then, a(n) is the least novel multiple of the greatest such prime p.
text: The sequence is conjectured to be a permutation of the positive integers with the primes appearing in their natural order.

name: Expansion of g.f. A(x) satisfying A(x) = Sum_{n>=0} d^n/dx^n (x^(5*n) * A(x)^n) / n!.
text: Conjecture: If r>=2 and s>=1 and A(x) = Sum_{n>=0} d^n/dx^n x^(r*n) * A(x)^(s*n) / n!, then a(n) ~ c(r,s) * n! * n^alpha(r,s) * ((r-1)/LambertW(1/s))^n, where alpha(r,s) = ((2*s+1)*LambertW(1/s) + 1 + 1/(1 + LambertW(1/s))) * r/(2*(r-1)) - 1 and c(r,s) is a constant independent on n. - _Vaclav Kotesovec_, Mar 16 2023
author: Vaclav Kotesovec

name: Expansion of g.f. A(x) satisfying 2*x = Sum_{n=-oo..+oo} x^(n*(3*n+1)/2) * (A(x)^(3*n) - 1/A(x)^(3*n+1)).
text: Conjecture: a(n) == A359914(n-1) (mod 4) for n > 1.

name: Expansion of g.f. A(x) satisfying 2*x = Sum_{n=-oo..+oo} x^(n*(3*n+1)/2) * (A(x)^(3*n) - 1/A(x)^(3*n+1)).
text: Conjecture: a(n)/2 == A000041(n-1) (mod 2) for n >= 1; that is, a(n) is even, and a(n)/2 has the same parity as the number of partitions of n-1, for n >= 1.

name: Positive integers such that GCD(A007504(n),n) != 1.
text: Conjecture: a(n) ~ C*n as n -> infinity, where 5.25 < C < 5.35.

name: For n <= 2, a(n) = n. Thereafter let p be the greatest prime which divides the least number of terms in U = {a(n-2), a(n-1)}, then a(n) is the smallest multiple of p that is not yet in the sequence.
text: Conjectured to be a permutation of the positive integers with primes in order.

name: a(n) is the least k such that tau(k) divides sigma_n(k) but not sigma(k), or -1 if no such k exists.
text: Conjecture: a(n) is of the form 2^b*p1^c*p2^d*...*pk^j with b > 0 and A020639(n) divides b*(c+1)*(d+1)*...*(j+1). (p1, p2, ..., pk are distinct odd prime numbers). (End)

name: a(n) is the least k such that tau(k) divides sigma_n(k) but not sigma(k), or -1 if no such k exists.
text: Conjecture: For primes q > p, a(q) > a(p). If true, we could replace "<=" with "=" in the above formula. (End)

name: a(n) = Sum_{k = 0..n-1} (-1)^k*binomial(n,k)*binomial(n-1,k)^2.
text: Conjecture: the supercongruence a(n*p^k) == a(n*p^(k-1)) (mod p^(3*k)) holds for all primes p >= 5 and positive integers n and k.

name: a(1) = 1 and a(n) = Sum_{k = 0..n-2} (-1)^k * binomial(n,k)^2 * binomial(n-2,k) for n >= 2.
text: Conjecture: the supercongruence a(p^k) == a(p^(k-1)) (mod p^(3*k)) holds for all primes p >= 5 and positive integer k.

name: a(n) = Sum_{k = 0..n-1} binomial(n,k)^2*binomial(n+k,k)*binomial(n+k-1,k).
text: Conjecture 1: the supercongruence a(p) == a(1) (mod p^5) holds for all primes p >= 7 (checked up to p = 199).

name: a(n) = Sum_{k = 0..n-1} binomial(n,k)^2*binomial(n+k,k)*binomial(n+k-1,k).
text: Conjecture 2: for r >= 2, the supercongruence a(p^r) == a(p^(r-1)) (mod p^(3*r+3)) holds for all primes p >= 5.

name: a(n) = Sum_{k = 0..n-1} binomial(n,k)^2 * binomial(n+k-1,k)^2.
text: Conjecture 1: the supercongruence a(p) == a(1) (mod p^5) holds for all primes p >= 7 (checked up to p = 199). Conjecture 2: for r >= 2, the supercongruence a(p^r) == a(p^(r-1)) (mod p^(4*r+1)) holds for all primes p >= 7. [added Aug 12 2026: The first conjecture is correct. The second conjecture is not correct as it stands - Thomas Adamczewski notes that a(7^6) - a(7^5) is divisible by 7^24 but not by 7^25.] Compare with the Apéry numbers A005259(n) = Sum_{k = 0..n} binomial(n,k)^2 * binomial(n+k,k)^2, which satisfy the weaker supercongruences A005259(p^r) == A005259(p^(r-1)) (mod p^(3*r)) for all positive integers r and all primes p >= 5. Adamczewski disproves Conjecture 2 in linked article. - _Michael De Vlieger_, Aug 18 2026
author: Michael De Vlieger

name: a(n) = Sum_{k = 0..n-1} binomial(n,k)^2 * binomial(n+k-1,k)^2.
text: Conjecture 2: for r >= 2, the supercongruence a(p^r) == a(p^(r-1)) (mod p^(4*r+1)) holds for all primes p >= 7. [added Aug 12 2026: The first conjecture is correct. The second conjecture is not correct as it stands - Thomas Adamczewski notes that a(7^6) - a(7^5) is divisible by 7^24 but not by 7^25.] Compare with the Apéry numbers A005259(n) = Sum_{k = 0..n} binomial(n,k)^2 * binomial(n+k,k)^2, which satisfy the weaker supercongruences A005259(p^r) == A005259(p^(r-1)) (mod p^(3*r)) for all positive integers r and all primes p >= 5. Adamczewski disproves Conjecture 2 in linked article. - _Michael De Vlieger_, Aug 18 2026
author: Michael De Vlieger

name: a(n) = Sum_{k = 0..n-1} binomial(n,k)^2 * binomial(n+k-1,k)^2.
text: Adamczewski disproves Conjecture 2 in linked article. - _Michael De Vlieger_, Aug 18 2026
author: Michael De Vlieger

name: a(n) = Sum_{k = 0..n-1} (-1)^(n+k+1)*binomial(n,k)*binomial(n+k-1,k)^2.
text: Conjecture 1: the supercongruence a(p) == a(1) (mod p^5) holds for all primes p >= 7 (checked up to p = 199). Conjecture 2: for r >= 2, the supercongruence a(p^r) == a(p^(r-1)) (mod p^(3*r+3)) holds for all primes p >= 7. Conjectures 1 and 2 are true: a(p) == a(1) (mod p^5) and a(p^r) == a(p^(r-1)) (mod p^(3*r+3)) for r >= 2 and all primes p >= 7 (see Theorem 1 in the Blanco Gómez link). - _Roberto Blanco Gómez_, Oct 18 2026
author: Roberto Blanco Gómez

name: a(n) = Sum_{k = 0..n-1} (-1)^(n+k+1)*binomial(n,k)*binomial(n+k-1,k)^2.
text: Conjecture 2: for r >= 2, the supercongruence a(p^r) == a(p^(r-1)) (mod p^(3*r+3)) holds for all primes p >= 7. Conjectures 1 and 2 are true: a(p) == a(1) (mod p^5) and a(p^r) == a(p^(r-1)) (mod p^(3*r+3)) for r >= 2 and all primes p >= 7 (see Theorem 1 in the Blanco Gómez link). - _Roberto Blanco Gómez_, Oct 18 2026
author: Roberto Blanco Gómez

author: Roberto Blanco Gómez

name: a(n) = Sum_{k = 0..n-1} binomial(n,k)^2*binomial(n+k-1,k).
text: Conjecture 1: the supercongruence a(p) == a(1) (mod p^5) holds for all primes p >= 7 (checked up to p = 199) [added Aug 15 2026: this is correct - see the Bala link.].

name: a(n) = Sum_{k = 0..n-1} binomial(n,k)^2*binomial(n+k-1,k).
text: Conjecture 2: for r >= 2, the supercongruence a(p^r) == a(p^(r-1)) (mod p^(3*r+3)) holds for all primes p >= 5.

name: a(n) = Sum_{k = 0..n-1} (-1)^k*binomial(n,k)^2*binomial(n-1,k).
text: Conjecture: the supercongruence a(n*p^k) == a(n*p^(k-1)) (mod p^(3*k)) holds for all primes p >= 5 and positive integers n and k.

name: a(n) = Sum_{k = 0..n-1} binomial(n-1,k)^2*binomial(n+k,k).
text: Conjecture 1: the supercongruence a(p) == 0 (mod p^4) holds for all primes p >= 5 (checked up to p = 199).

name: a(n) = Sum_{k = 0..n-1} binomial(n-1,k)^2*binomial(n+k,k).
text: Conjecture 2: the supercongruence a(p-1) == 1 - 2*p - p^2 (mod p^3) holds for all primes except p = 3 (checked up to p = 199).

name: Lexicographically earliest sequence of distinct positive integers such that a(n) and a(n-1) share at least one identical trit at the same position in their balanced ternary representations.
text: Conjecture: Suppose n is the x-th fixed point such that n-1 is not a fixed point. Then for all k such that n < k < (3^(x + 2) + 1)/2, k is also a fixed point.

name: a(1) = 1, a(2) = 2; for n > 2, a(n) is the smallest positive number that has not yet appeared that is a multiple of the smallest prime that does not divide a(n-2) + a(n-1).
text: The sequence is conjectured to be a permutation of the positive integers, although it takes many terms for the primes to appear, e.g., a(191443) = 19.

name: a(n) is equal to the number of roots of the equation n*cos(x) = sqrt(x).
text: Conjecture: a(n) = 2*floor(n^2/(2*Pi)) + 1.

name: a(n) is the first member of A106843 with sum of digits n.
text: Conjecture: a(n) == 9 (mod 10) for all n > 25. Conjecture: all terms are zeroless. - _Chai Wah Wu_, Mar 30 2023
author: Chai Wah Wu

name: a(n) is the first member of A106843 with sum of digits n.
text: Conjecture: all terms are zeroless. - _Chai Wah Wu_, Mar 30 2023
author: Chai Wah Wu

name: a(n) = (1/n) * Sum_{k = 0..n} (n+2*k) * binomial(n+k-1,k)^3.
text: The central binomial coefficients u(n) := binomial(2*n,n) = A000984(n) satisfy the supercongruences u(n*p^r) == u(n*p^(r-1)) (mod p^(3*r)) for positive integers n and r and all primes p >= 5. We conjecture that the present sequence satisfies the same congruences. More generally, for m >= 3, the sequences {b_m(n) : n >= 1} and {c_m(n) : n >= 1} defined by b_m(n) = (1/n) * Sum_{k = 0..n} (n + 2*k) * binomial(n+k-1,k)^m and c_m(n) = (1/n) * Sum_{k = 0..n} (-1)^k * (n + 2*k) * binomial(n+k-1,k)^m may satisfy the same congruences. Adamczewski includes a proof abstract of the above conjecture in linked article. - _Michael De Vlieger_, Aug 18 2026
author: Michael De Vlieger

name: a(n) = (1/n) * Sum_{k = 0..n} (n+2*k) * binomial(n+k-1,k)^3.
text: Adamczewski includes a proof abstract of the above conjecture in linked article. - _Michael De Vlieger_, Aug 18 2026

name: a(n) = (1/n) * Sum_{k = 0..2*n} (n+2*k) * binomial(n+k-1,k)^3.
text: The binomial coefficients u(n) := binomial(3*n,n) = A005809(n) satisfy the supercongruences u(n*p^r) == u(n*p^(r-1)) (mod p^(3*r)) for positive integers n and r and all primes p >= 5. We conjecture that the present sequence satisfies the same congruences.

name: a(n) = (1/n) * Sum_{k = 0..2*n} (-1)^k * (n+2*k) * binomial(n+k-1,k)^3.
text: The binomial coefficients u(n) := binomial(3*n,n) = A005809(n) satisfy the supercongruences u(n*p^r) == u(n*p^(r-1)) (mod p^(3*r)) for positive integers n and r and all primes p >= 5. We conjecture that the present sequence satisfies the same congruences.

name: a(n) = S(5,n), where S(r,n) = Sum_{k = 0..floor(n/2)} ( binomial(n,k) - binomial(n,k-1) )^r.
text: For r a positive integer define S(r,n) = Sum_{k = 0..floor(n/2)} ( binomial(n,k) - binomial(n,k-1) )^r. The present sequence is {S(5,n)}. Gould (1974) conjectured that S(3,n) was always divisible by S(1,n). See A183069 for {S(3,n)/S(1,n)}. In fact, calculation suggests that if r is odd then S(r,n) is always divisible by S(1,n). a(n) is the total number of 5-tuples of semi-Dyck paths from (0,0) to (n,n-2*j) for j=0..floor(n/2). - _Alois P. Heinz_, Apr 02 2023
author: Alois P. Heinz

name: a(n) = S(5,n)/S(1,n), where S(r,n) = Sum_{k = 0..floor(n/2)} ( binomial(n,k) - binomial(n,k-1) )^r.
text: For r a positive integer define S(r,n) = Sum_{k = 0..floor(n/2)} ( binomial(n,k) - binomial(n,k-1) )^r. Gould (1974) conjectured that S(3,n) was always divisible by S(1,n). name: a(n) = S(5,2*n-1)/S(1,2*n-1), where S(r,n) = Sum_{k = 0..floor(n/2)} ( binomial(n,k) - binomial(n,k-1) )^r.
text: Conjecture: the supercongruence a(n*p^r) == a(n*p^(r-1)) (mod p^(3*r)) holds for positive integers n and r and all primes p >= 5.

name: a(n) = S(7,n), where S(r,n) = Sum_{k = 0..floor(n/2)} ( binomial(n,k) - binomial(n,k-1) )^r.

See A183069 for {S(3,n)/S(1,n)}. In fact, calculation suggests that if r is odd then S(r,n) is always divisible by S(1,n). The present sequence is {S(7,n)/S(1,n)}.

name: a(n) = S(7,2*n-1)/S(1,2*n-1), where S(r,n) = Sum_{k = 0..floor(n/2)} ( binomial(n,k) - binomial(n,k-1) )^r.
text: Conjecture: the supercongruence a(n*p^r) == a(n*p^(r-1)) (mod p^(3*r)) holds for positive integers n and r and all primes p >= 5.

name: Leading terms of the rows of the array in A362450; or, Gilbreath transform of tau (A000005).
text: Conjecture: All terms are either 0 or 1. Verified to a(10^7). Inspired by Gilbreath's conjecture, A036262. Using the terminology of A362451, this is the Gilbreath transform of tau (A000005). - _N. J. A. Sloane_, May 05 2023
author: N. J. A. Sloane

name: Leading terms of the rows of the array in A362450; or, Gilbreath transform of tau (A000005).
text: Inspired by Gilbreath's conjecture, A036262. Using the terminology of A362451, this is the Gilbreath transform of tau (A000005). - _N. J. A. Sloane_, May 05 2023
author: N. J. A. Sloane

name: Odd numbers k such that for all even divisors d of k^2+1, d^2+1 is a prime number.
text: Conjecture: the sequence is infinite.

name: Primes that are repunits with three or more digits for exactly one base b >= 2.
text: Equals A085104 \ {31, 8191}, since according to the Goormaghtigh conjecture (link), 31 and 8191 which are both Mersenne numbers, are the only primes which are Brazilian in two different bases.

name: The number of primes > A000040(n) and <= (A000040(n)^c + 1)^(1/c), where c = 0.567148130202... is defined in A038458.
text: Let c = 0.567148130202... (see A038458), the solution to 127^x - 113^x = 1. c is conjectured by Smarandache to be the smallest real number x such that A000040(n+1)^x - A000040(n)^x = 1 has a solution. This conjecture is equivalent to saying that the terms of the present sequence are always positive, but that if c were replaced by a larger real number, there would be zeros in the sequence. However, note that a(30) is not the last occurrence of 1: a(46) = a(61) = 1 as well.

name: a(1) = 2; for n > 1, a(n) is the smallest positive integer > 1 not to share a factor with terms a(n-c .. n-1) where c = gcd(n-1,a(n-1)).
text: Conjecture: All primes will occur. See A361931 for the first occurrences of primes.

name: a(n) is the greatest prime p such that p + q^2 + r^3 = prime(n)^4 for some primes q and r.
text: Conjecture: a(n) exists for all n > 2.

name: a(n) is the smallest number k such that A361929(k) = prime(n), or -1 if no such prime exists.
text: It is conjectured that all primes appear in A361929.

name: Total semiperimeter of 3-Fuss-Catalan polyominoes of length 3n.
Numbers k with a single solution x to the equation uphi(x) = k, where uphi is the unitary totient function (A047994).
text: According to Carmichael's totient function conjecture, there are no numbers with a single solution x to the corresponding equation phi(x) = k, with Euler's totient function (A000010).

name: Numbers k such that the digits of k^2 are a subsequence of the digits of 2^k.
text: Conjecture is true up to 10^6. - _Michael S. Branicky_, Apr 03 2023
author: Michael S. Branicky

name: a(n) is the minimum integer m such that floor(e^n) = floor(Sum_{k=0..m} (n^k)/(k!)).
text: Conjecture: a(n) ~ e*n as n->infinity.

name: a(n) is the minimum integer m such that floor(e^n) = floor(Sum_{k=0..m} (n^k)/(k!)).
text: Conjecture: a(n) <= 3n for all n.

name: a(n) is the leading prime in the n-th prime sublist defined in A348168.
text: If Conjecture 2 in A348168 is true, lim_{n->infinity} a(n)/prime(round((n-1)*e)+1) = 1, where e is Euler's number. If a term p (>2) is from a single-prime sublist (A356271), then p is a weak prime (A051635) or a balanced prime (A006562). Otherwise, p is a strong prime (A051634). The definition divides the primes into maximal sublists such that gaps between adjacent primes in a sublist are smaller than the gap that precedes the sublist and no larger than the first gap within the sublist. - _Peter Munn_, Jul 07 2025
author: Peter Munn

name: Numbers k such that the digits of k^2 do not form a subsequence of the digits of 2^k.
text: Complement of A362001. It was conjectured that a(140)=327 is the last term (see A362001).

name: Lexicographically least counterexample to Dombi's conjecture.
text: Dombi's conjecture, now refuted, stated that there is no infinite set A such that the power series (sum(X^a, a>=0 not in A))^3 has strictly increasing coefficients. This sequence is conjecturally the lexicographically least such example---"conjecturally" because it is obtained by backtracking and there is currently no proof it can be extended to infinity.

name: Write the English name of a(n); sum the ranks of its letters in the alphabet; divide the sum by a(n); the result is an integer.
text: Indices of zeros in A226911; and conjectured finite, full based on an observation there. - _Michael S. Branicky_, Apr 07 2023
author: Michael S. Branicky

name: Numbers k such that k + digitsum(k^2) is a square.
text: Conjecture: there are infinitely many pairs of consecutive terms. Example: (296,297); (413,414); (863,864).

name: Let m_min(n, k) be the smallest m such that n divides Product_{t=1..m} RisingFactorial(t, k). a(n) = Sum_{r=1..K(n)} m_min(n, r), where K(n) is the Kempner number A002034(n).
text: Conjecture: the equation a(n) = a(n+1) has no solutions. This holds up to at least n = 10^4.

name: Let m_min(n, k) be the smallest m such that n divides Product_{t=1..m} RisingFactorial(t, k). a(n) = Sum_{r=1..K(n)} m_min(n, r), where K(n) is the Kempner number A002034(n).
text: Conjecture: the constant Sum_{n >= 2} 1/a(n)! = 0.16945... is irrational.

name: Denominator of the continued fraction 1/(2-3/(3-4/(4-5/(...(n-1)-n/(-3))))).
text: Conjecture: Except for 9, every term of this sequence is either a prime or 1. Conjecture: Record values correspond to A248697 (n>3). - _Bill McEachen_, Mar 06 2024
author: Bill McEachen

name: Denominator of the continued fraction 1/(2-3/(3-4/(4-5/(...(n-1)-n/(-3))))).
text: Conjecture: Record values correspond to A248697 (n>3). - _Bill McEachen_, Mar 06 2024
author: Bill McEachen

name: Numbers that take a record number of steps to appear in the Sisyphus sequence A350877.
text: It is conjectured that every number will eventually appear in A350877. The terms in this sequence are the numbers that are the slowest to appear. For example, 115 does not appear until term 45274461582754.

name: Decimal expansion of K, a constant arising in the analysis of the binary Euclidean algorithm.
text: Vallée (1998) conjectured that this constant times A362150 equals 4*log(2)/Pi^2; Brent (1999) supported the conjecture with numerical computations and Morris (2016) proved the conjecture.

name: a(n) = the hypergraph Catalan number C_2(n).
text: Gunnells gives several combinatorial interpretations of the hypergraph Catalan numbers, a method to compute their generating functions to arbitrary precision and some conjectural asymptotics.

name: a(n) = the hypergraph Catalan number C_2(n).
text: a(n) ~ e^(3/2) * 2^(n+1) * n!/sqrt(Pi*n) (conjectural).

name: a(n) = the hypergraph Catalan number C_3(n).
text: Gunnells gives several combinatorial interpretations of the hypergraph Catalan numbers, a method to compute their generating functions to arbitrary precision and some conjectural asymptotics.

name: a(n) = the hypergraph Catalan number C_3(n).
text: a(n) ~ sqrt(3) * (9/2)^n * n!^2/(Pi*n) (conjectural).

name: a(n) = the hypergraph Catalan number C_4(n).
text: Gunnells gives several combinatorial interpretations of the hypergraph Catalan numbers, a method to compute their generating functions to arbitrary precision and some conjectural asymptotics.

name: a(n) = the hypergraph Catalan number C_4(n).
text: a(n) ~ sqrt(2) * (32/3)^n * n!^3/(Pi*n)^(3/2) (conjectural).

name: a(n) = the hypergraph Catalan number C_5(n).
text: Gunnells gives several combinatorial interpretations of the hypergraph Catalan numbers, a method to compute their generating functions to arbitrary precision and some conjectural asymptotics.

name: a(n) = the hypergraph Catalan number C_5(n).
text: a(n) ~ sqrt(5)/2 * (5^4/24)^n * n!^4/(Pi*n)^2 (conjectural).

name: a(n) = the hypergraph Catalan number C_6(n).
text: Gunnells gives several combinatorial interpretations of the hypergraph Catalan numbers, a method to compute their generating functions to arbitrary precision and some conjectural asymptotics.

name: a(n) = the hypergraph Catalan number C_6(n).
a(n) = the hypergraph Catalan number C_7(n).
text: Gunnells gives several combinatorial interpretations of the hypergraph Catalan numbers, a method to compute their generating functions to arbitrary precision and some conjectural asymptotics.

name: a(n) = the hypergraph Catalan number C_7(n).
text: a(n) ~ sqrt(7)/4 * (7^6/6!)^n * n!^6/(Pi*n)^3 (conjectural).

name: Lexicographically earliest sequence of distinct nonnegative integers having the same concatenation of digits as the sequence 2^a(n).
text: We conjecture that this is a permutation of the nonnegative integers, but a proof seems without reach. Can it be disproved?

name: Lexicographic earliest sequence of distinct positive integers having the same concatenation of digits as the sequence 2^a(n).
text: We conjecture that this is a permutation of the positive integers, but a proof seems without reach. Can it be disproved?

name: a(n) is the number of locations 1..n-1 which can reach i=n-1, where jumps from location i to i +- a(i) are permitted (within 1..n-1); a(1)=1. See example.
text: Conjecture: a(n) is also the largest number such that starting point i=n can reach every previous location (with a(1)=1 and the same rule for jumps as in the current name).

name: Numbers > 9 with increasingly large digit average of their square, in base 10.
text: It is conjectured but not known that there are only finitely many numbers whose square has a digit average above 8.3.

name: a(n) = A000010(n) + A000010(n+2), where A000010 is the Euler phi-function.
text: Conjecture: a(2*n) <= a(2*n-1) and a(2*n) < a(2*n+1).

name: a(0) = 0; for n > 0, if n appears in the sequence then a(n) is the sum of the indices of all previous appearances of n. Otherwise a(n) = a(n-1) - n if nonnegative and not already in the sequence, otherwise a(n) = a(n-1) + n.
text: Conjecture: All nonnegative integers appear in this sequence. - _Yifan Xie_, Apr 24 2023
author: Yifan Xie

name: Denominators of the expansion of the series reversion of sin(x) + x, odd powers only.
Numerators of the expansion of the series reversion of sin(x) + x, odd powers only.
text: Conjecture: a(n) = abs(A302977(n)).

name: a(n) = [x^n] (F(x)/F(-x))^n where F(x) = (1 + x)*(1 + x^3).
text: Let k and m be positive integers and let f(x) be a finite product of cyclotomic polynomials. Define b(n) = [x^(k*n)] (f(x)/f(-x))^(m*n). Then we conjecture that the supercongruences a(p) == a(1) (mod p^3) and, for n >= 2, a(n*p) == a(n) (mod p^2) hold for all primes p, with a finite number of exceptions depending on f(x).

name: a(n) = [x^n] (F(x)/F(-x))^n where F(x) = (1 + x)*(1 + x^3).
text: Conjectures: 1) the supercongruence a(p) == 2 (mod p^3) holds for all primes p >= 5 (checked up to p = 47).

name: Numbers that can be written as A000045(i) + j^2 for i,j>=0 in 4 ways.
text: Conjecture: a(n) = 1 + A000045(6*n)^2/4. Conjecture: Sum_{n>=1} 1/a(n) = sqrt(5)/4 - 1/2 (true if the above formula is valid). - _Amiram Eldar_, Dec 25 2025
author: Amiram Eldar

name: Numbers that can be written as A000045(i) + j^2 for i,j>=0 in 4 ways.
text: Conjecture: Sum_{n>=1} 1/a(n) = sqrt(5)/4 - 1/2 (true if the above formula is valid). - _Amiram Eldar_, Dec 25 2025
author: Amiram Eldar

name: Array of numbers read by upward antidiagonals: leading row lists tau(i), i >= 1 (cf. A000005);  the following rows give absolute values of differences of previous row.
text: Analogous to the array in A036262 that arises from Gilbreath's conjecture.

name: Array of numbers read by upward antidiagonals: leading row lists tau(i), i >= 1 (cf. A000005);  the following rows give absolute values of differences of previous row.
text: Wayman Eduardo Luy and _Robert G. Wilson v_ conjecture (see A361897) that the leading terms in the array are always 0 or 1.

name: a(n) = A054978(n)/2 if that number is 0 or 1, otherwise -1.
text: Conjectured to be always 0 or 1.

name: Array of numbers read by upward antidiagonals: leading row lists the primes as they were in the 19th century (A008578); the following rows give absolute values of differences of previous row.
text: Analogous to A036262. The Gilbreath conjecture is that the initial terms of the rows are 1,(1,0)* = A135528.

name: a(n) is the least number of 2 or more consecutive signed primes whose sum equals n.
text: Inspired by a conjecture made by Carlos Rivera in 2000 (see link). Here we remove Rivera's restriction that the primes have to be smaller than n.

name: a(n) is the least number of 2 or more consecutive signed primes whose sum equals n.
text: For every positive even n, a(n) = 2, provided there are 2 consecutive primes separated by a gap of size n. Polignac's conjecture says: "For any positive even number n, there are infinitely many prime gaps of size n." If so, a(3) is the only 4 in this sequence, as any even number of consecutive odd signed primes has an even sum.

name: First occurrence of n in A362465 or -1 if n is not a term in A362465.
text: All terms a(n) for even n > 4 are conjectures and conjectured to be -1. This follows from the reason derived from Polignac's conjecture that is described in A362465.

name: First occurrence of n in A362465 or -1 if n is not a term in A362465.
text: The requirements for the truth of the above conjecture about this sequence seem to be notably weaker than for Polignac's conjecture.

name: a(1) = 2 and a(n+1) is the largest prime <= a(n) + n.
text: Conjecture: a(n+1) > a(n). The conjecture holds for the first 2^32.5 =~ 6074001000 terms as all prime gaps up to 2^64 are known. - _Charles R Greathouse IV_, Apr 27 2023
author: Charles R Greathouse IV

name: a(1) = 2 and a(n+1) is the largest prime <= a(n) + n.
text: The conjecture holds for the first 2^32.5 =~ 6074001000 terms as all prime gaps up to 2^64 are known. - _Charles R Greathouse IV_, Apr 27 2023
author: Charles R Greathouse IV

name: a(1) = 2 and a(n+1) is the largest prime <= a(n) + n.
text: The conjecture is true since prime(n+1)<=prime(n)+n. See for example Theorem 2 in Torelli (2006). - _Mauro Torelli_, Sep 30 2026
author: Mauro Torelli

name: Numbers that can be written in at least 3 ways as the sum of a Lucas number (A000032) and a square.
text: Conjecture: there are never more than 3 solutions.

name: Numerators of the ratio of the symmetry-constrained bound to the adiabatic bound on polarization transfer in AXn spin-1/2 systems.
text: Conjecture: the numerator of g(n) is the denominator of f(n)/g(n).

name: a(n) = n for n <= 2. For n > 2, a(n) is the least novel k (with rad(k) != rad(a(n-1))) such that k shares a nontrivial divisor with one of a(n-1), a(n-2), but not with the other.
text: Conjectured to be a permutation of the positive integers in which the primes appear in natural order.

name: Number of integer partitions of n whose weighted sum is divisible by n.
text: Conjecture: A partition of n has weighted sum divisible by n iff its reverse has weighted sum divisible by n.

name: Number of integer partitions of n whose weighted sum is not divisible by n.
text: Conjecture: A partition of n has weighted sum divisible by n iff its reverse has weighted sum divisible by n.

name: Integers in the interval [Pi*k - 1/k, Pi*k + 1/k] for some k > 0 that are numerators of convergents to 2*Pi.
text: Conjecture: the sequence is infinite.

name: Lexicographically earliest sequence of distinct positive terms such that for any n > 0, the initial digit "d" of a(n) divides a(n+d).
text: Conjecture: For n > 68, a(n) < 3*n. - _Charles R Greathouse IV_, Mar 13 2025
author: Charles R Greathouse IV

name: Least prime pn such that there is a set p1 < p2 < ... < pn of primes such that, for any distinct p and q in the set, p + q + 1 is prime.
text: Balog shows that a(n) exists for each n. On Dickson's conjecture, Tao & Ziegler show that there is an infinite set S with this property.

name: Lexicographically earliest infinite sequence of distinct positive integers with a(n) = n for n <= 3, and for n > 3  a(n) is the least novel multiple of the greatest prime divisor of a(n-2) which does not divide a(n-1).
text: Conjectured to be a permutation of the positive integers with the primes in order.

name: a(n) = Sum_{k = 0..n} 4^(n-k)*binomial(n,k)*binomial(n-1,k)*binomial(2*k,k).
text: The Franel numbers satisfy the supercongruences u(n*p^r) == u(n*p^(r-1)) (mod p^(3*r)) for all primes p >= 5 and positive integers n and r. We conjecture that the present sequence satisfies the same supercongruences. From _Peter Bala_, Jul 07 2023 (Start):
author: Peter Bala

name: a(n) = Sum_{k = 0..n} 4^(n-k)*binomial(n,k)*binomial(n-1,k)*binomial(2*k,k).
text: We conjecture that the present sequence satisfies the same supercongruences. (End)

name: a(n) is the permanent of the n X n symmetric matrix M(n) defined by M[i, j, n] = min(i, j)*(n + 1) - i*j.
text: Conjecture: det(M(n)) = A000272(n+1). The conjecture is true (see proof in Links). - _Stefano Spezia_, May 24 2023
author: Stefano Spezia

author: Stefano Spezia

text: Conjecture by Andrew Young: For an n X n square, where n is an odd prime, there is only one n-cell pattern. Conjecture by Andrew Young and Thomas Young: An odd integer n>=3 is prime iff there exists only one n-cell pattern for an n X n square. For any number n, there is always the 1 X n pattern that tiles the n X n square. For composite numbers n = f1*f2, 1 < f1 <= f2 < n, there is always an additional f1 X f2 pattern. For example, a 14 X 14 square can be tiled using fourteen 1 X 14 rectangles or fourteen 2 X 7 rectangles; a 15 X 15 square can be tiled using fifteen 1 X 15 rectangles or fifteen 3 X 5 rectangles; a 9 X 9 square can be tiled using nine 1 X 9 rectangles or nine 3 X 3 squares (as in Sudoku!). The second conjecture is a Corollary of the first: If n = p*q is not prime, then there is always a second tiling using rectangles, as explained above. Since the second conjecture implies the first, the two conjectures are actually equivalent. - _M. F. Hasler_, Jun 15 2025

name: a(1) = 1. Thereafter, a(n) is the least novel multiple of either prime(k+1) if rad(a(n-1)) = A002110(k), or Product_{prime q; q < gpf(a(n-1)); and q!|a(n-1)} q otherwise.
text: In other words, if the squarefree kernel of a(n-1) is a primorial term then a(n) is the least novel multiple of the smallest prime which does not divide a(n-1). Otherwise a(n) is the least novel multiple of the product of all primes < gpf(a(n-1)) which do not divide a(n-1). Primes >= 5 arrive late (as least unused term), and a(k) is prime(m) iff a(k-1) is A002110(m-1). The pattern around a prime is P(k), prime(k+1), 2*P(k), m*prime(k+1) for some multiplier m, where P(k) = A002110(k). The sequence is conjectured to be a permutation of the positive integers, with primes in natural order. A common mode in this sequence is alternation of squarefree semiprime q(j)*q(k), j < k, followed by P(k-1)/q(j). The alternation often occurs in runs such that each iteration increments k. Example: a(241..246): q(2)*q(17) -> P(16)/q(2) -> q(2)*q(18) -> P(17)/q(2) -> q(2)*q(19) -> P(18)/q(2). a(16539..16572) represents a run of 17 alternations. - _Michael De Vlieger_, Jul 17 2023

name: An irregular triangle read by rows, the 3rd row-symmetric Fibonaccian triangle: T(n,k) is the Whitney number of level k of the (3,n)-th symmetric Fibonaccian lattice (0 <= n, 0 <= k <= 2*n).
text: In [Donnelly, Dunkum, Lišková, and Nance, 2023], the (m,n)-th symmetric Fibonaccian lattice L is also described using semistandard tableaux of a specific ribbon shape; the irreducible components of the associated sl(m,C)-representation are in one-to-one correspondence with what are called the 'ballot-admissible' (aka Littlewood-Richardson) tableaux. In terms of Fibonaccian strings, an element S = (S(1),...,S(n)) in L is ballot-admissible iff for any integer q between 1 and n (inclusive) and any integer r between 1 and m-1 (inclusive), the following integer quantity is nonnegative: Sum_{k=n+1-q..n}([n+1-k is odd]*([r+(k-1)*m = S(k)] - [r+(k-1)*m+1 = S(k)]) + [n+1-k is even]*([k*m-r = S(k)]-[k*m+1-r = S(k)])), where '[]' denotes the Iverson bracket. Enumerating the ballot-admissible tableaux or Fibonaccian strings in L seems to be an interesting problem when m >= 3; when m=3, the sizes of the sets of ballot-admissible tableaux conjecturally agree with A004148.

name: For n >= 3, r >= 0, y an integer, a(n) is the number of integral solutions to the elliptic equation y^2 = n^3 + n^2 + 2*r*n + r^2.
text: Factoring the equation y^2 = n^3 + n^2 + 2*r*n + r^2 yields (y+n+r)*(y-n-r) = n^3, which implies y+n+r = d and y-n-r = n^3/d for some divisor d of n^3.  Thus a(n) is the number of divisors d of n^3 such that (d-n^3/d)/2 - n is a nonnegative integer.  This resolves some of Thomas Scheuerle's conjectures. - _Robin Visser_, Sep 30 2023

name: Irregular triangle read by rows: T(n,k) = A237591(n,k) - A237591(n-1,k).
text: Conjecture: column k gives 1 together with period A002378(k) repeat S_k, where S_k is the k-th row of the triangle A364746. Some connections with other sequences are as follows: n is a power of 2 (A000079) if and only if row n is [1] or if row n starts with 1 and the remaining terms are zeros. n is an odd prime (A065091) if and only if row n is [0, 1] or if row n starts with [0, 1] and the remaining terms are zeros. n is a nonzero multiple of 6 (A008588 > 0) if and only if row n starts with [1, -1]. n is an even perfect number (A000396 assuming there are no odd perfect numbers) if and only if row n is [1, -1, 1] or if row n starts with [1] and ends in [-1, 1] and the remaining terms are zeros and row n has an odd number of terms and row n-1 has an even number of terms. n is a term >= 10 of A091999 (and thus n is also a term >= 10 of A063221) if and only if row n starts with [1, 0, -1]. n is a term of A362866 (or, equivalently, a prime doubled (A100484) >= 10, also an even semiprime >= 10) if and only if row n is [1, 0, -1, 1] or if row n starts with [1, 0, -1, 1] and the remaining terms are zeros. n is a term of A364414 if and only if row n starts with [0, 0, 1, 0, -1]. n is a term of A365081 if and only if row n is [0, 0, 1, 0, -1, 1] or if row n starts with [0, 0, 1, 0, -1, 1] and the remaining terms are zeros. T(n,k) is also the difference between the length of the k-th line segment of the largest Dyck path of the symmetric representation of sigma(n) and the length of the k-th line segment of its smallest Dyck paths, from left to the axis of symmetry. For further information about these Dyck paths see A237593. The partial sums of column k give the k-th column of A237591. Since A237591 can be defined using partitions into consecutive parts (see A299765 and A286000), this sequence can be associated to partitions of that kind. All connections mentioned above are due to the connections between geometry and number theory given by the stepped pyramid described in A245092. The diagram called "symmetric representation of sigma(n)" is essentially the shape of the terraces in the n-th level starting from the top of the mentioned pyramid. From _Hartmut F. W. Hoft_, Aug 17 2024: (Start)

This says that between any two consecutive multiples of 210 the 48 values that are not divisible by 2, 3, 5 or 7 are equally distributed between 6 equal divisions of 210; that is, 8 are in the interval [0, 34], 8 in the interval [35, 69], etc. - _Peter Munn_, Feb 16 2024

name: Consider the Fermat quotient for base n: Fq(n,k) = (n^(p - 1) - 1)/p, where p = prime(k), for k >= 1. a(n) is the least k >= 1 such that Fq(n,j) is divisible by n^2 - 1 for all j >= k.
text: Conjecture: numbers appear in the sequence only a finite number of times. Terms appear in runs of length 1, 2, or 3, never more. The first time a term k appears is when the index is even. The terms appear for the first time in their natural order.

Then for n such that k_2 = 0 or k_3 = 0, a(n) = n, else a(n) is the least novel number Min{p*a(k_2), q*a(k_3)}, where p, q are primes not equal to either 2 or 3.
text: Conjectures: (i). This is a permutation of A047253 with primes in order; (ii). All terms between consecutive prime terms, prime(k), prime(k+1) are prime(k)-smooth.

text: Conjecture: This hailstone operation on odd prime numbers will always reach 3.

name: a(1) = 2; for n > 2, a(n) is the smallest positive number that has not yet appeared that is a multiple of A008472(a(n-1)), the sum of the distinct primes dividing a(n-1).
text: In the first 500000 terms the only fixed points are 38 and 209, although it is likely more exist. In the same range the smallest missing numbers are 311, 313, 337. The sequence is conjectured to be a permutation of the integers >= 2.

name: a(1) = 2; for n > 2, a(n) is the smallest positive number that has not yet appeared that has a common factor with A008472(a(n-1)), the sum of the distinct primes dividing a(n-1).
text: In the first 100000 terms the only fixed point is 9, and it is likely no more exist. In the same range the smallest missing numbers are 503, 839, 877. The sequence is conjectured to be a permutation of the integers >= 2.

name: a(n) is the least divisor (d) of prime(n)# such that prime(n)# / d + 1 is prime where p# denotes the product of all primes <= p.
text: Conjecture: a(n) < 2*prime(n).

name: Write out the canonical factorization of n and factorize the exponents in the factorization, the exponents in the factorizations of the exponents, ... until there are only prime numbers left. Replace each p in the factorization by (p-1)+1 and factorize each p-1 by the same process if p-1 > 1. Continue this process until there are only 1s left. a(n) is the number of 1s used.
text: Conjecture: for k >= 2, the maximum n such that a(n) = k is n = A001144(k). n = A365093(k) is the minimum such n.

name: Smallest k such that A365092(k) = n.
text: For m,n >= 2, it is easy to see that if gcd(a(m),a(n)) = 1, then a(m+n) <= a(m)*a(n). This is conjectured to be true for all m,n. In particular, it is conjectured that a(n+2) <= 2*a(n). If a(m+n) <= a(m)*a(n) is true, then by Fekete's subadditive lemma, we have lim_{n->oo} a(n)^(1/n) = inf_{n>=1} a(n)^(1/n) <= a(29)^(1/29) = 2879^(1/29) = 1.3160857758...

Conjecture 2: for n >= 2, if |Aut(G)| = a(n), then |G| = a(n)/p, where p = prime(n). Moreover, G is unique up to isomorphism if p == 2 (mod 3). Adamczewski includes a disproof abstract in the linked paper - _Michael De Vlieger_, Aug 17 2026.

name: Irregular triangle read by rows: T(n,k) is the number of partitions of n that have depth k.
text: Suppose that P is a partition of n. Let x(1), x(2),...,x(k) be the distinct parts of P, and let m(i) be the multiplicity of x(i) in P. Let f(P) be the partition [m(1)*x(1), m(2)*x(2),...,x(k)*m(k)] of n. Define c(0,P) = P, c(1,P) = f(P), ..., c(n,P) = f(c(n-1,P)), and define d(P) = least n such that c(n,P) has no repeated parts; d(P) is as the depth of P, as defined in A237685. Clearly d(P) = 0 if and only if P is a strict partition, as in A000009. Conjecture: if d >= 0, then 2^d is the least n that has a partition of depth d.

text: Conjecture: This is a permutation of the positive integers, with primes in order. Each prime p generates a trajectory T(p), dominated by multiples of p, see graph. Typically T(prime(k)) is initiated following the earliest term divisible by prime(k). Some trajectories are more prominent in the graph than others e.g. T(7),T(11),T(13) extend from p = prime(k) to prime(k+1)*prime(k). Others, e.g. T(3) terminate earlier but include prime(k)^2, whilst some do not reach as far as prime(k)^2 (T(5) has just two terms). Thus three categories of prime trajectory can be distinguished in the graph (respectively "full", "medium" and "small"). The graph resembles an inclined comb whose teeth correspond to full and medium trajectories; see Example.

name: Number of subsets of {1..n} whose cardinality is not the sum of two distinct elements.
text: The two conjectures of Chai Wah Wu above are true. Proof: write g(f,p,k) = [x^k] (1+2*x)^p*(1+x)^f and T_s(n) = Sum_{p=0..floor(n/2)} g(n-2*p, p, 2*p+s), so that a(n) = 1 + T_1(n) + T_2(n) by the formula above. Pascal's rule in f gives T_{s+1}(n+1) = T_{s+1}(n) + T_s(n), and in p it gives T_s(n+2) = binomial(n+2,s) + T_{s+2}(n) + 2*T_{s+1}(n). The first identity for s = 1, 2 and the second for s = 1 form a linear system from which the recurrence follows, and the initial terms 1, 2, 4, 7 then give the g.f. Both the formula and the recurrence are formalized in Lean 4 (see Links).

name: a(1) = 2; for n > 1, a(n) = a(n-1) + 2*gpf(a(n-1)), where gpf(k) = A006530(k) = greatest prime dividing k.
text: Conjecture: with the requirement that the prime factorization of each term is written so that the primes are ordered from smallest to largest, the sequence is the lexicographically earliest infinite sequence of distinct positive numbers such that gpf(a(n-1)) * lpf(a(n)) = |a(n) - a(n-1)|, where gpf(k) = A006530(k) = greatest prime factor of k and lpf(k) = A020639(k) = least prime factor of k. In this way the sequence is the ordered prime factorization version of the 'Commas sequence', A121805. One can show that, for such a sequence to be infinite, no odd number can appear. Although for many terms a lower even number can be chosen for the following term, which can lead to even lower numbers for further terms, it is conjectured all such choices will ultimately halt the sequence as a number is eventually reached for which no unused next number exists which follows the required rule for the difference between the terms. Therefore all terms must be larger than the previous, and the earliest such infinite sequence is the given sequence.

name: Number of representations of 4n-1 as a sum (p*q + p*r + q*r) with three odd primes p <= q <= r.
text: Goldbach's conjecture can be expressed by claiming that each even number > 4 is an arithmetic derivative of an odd semiprime, as (p*q)' = p+q, where p and q are odd primes. One way to extend Goldbach's conjecture to three primes involves applying the arithmetic derivative to all possible products of three odd primes (A046316) as: (p*q*r)' = (p*q) + (p*r) + (q*r), and asking, "Onto which subset of natural numbers does this map surjectively?" Clearly, the above formula can only produce numbers of the form 4m+3, and furthermore, an analysis at A369252 shows that the trisections of this sequence have quite different expected values, being on average the highest in the trisection A369462, which gives the number of representations for the numbers of the form 12m+11. This motivates a new kind of Goldbach-3 conjecture: "All numbers of the form 12*m-1, with m large enough, have at least one representation as a sum (p*q + p*r + q*r) with three odd primes p <= q <= r." Furthermore, empirical data for sequence A369463 suggests that "large enough" in this case might well be 4224080, as 1+(12*4224079) = 50688949 = A369463(285), with the next term of A369463 so far unknown. Similar conjectures can be envisaged for the arithmetic derivatives of products of four or more primes. - _Antti Karttunen_, Jan 25 2024

name: a(n) is the number of distinct elements appearing in the sequence formed by recursively applying A063655 when starting from n.
text: A063655(n) gives the smallest semiperimeter of an integral rectangle with area n, which is the same thing as the minimum sum of two positive integers whose product is n. In this sequence, A063655 is applied recursively until a cycle is found. Then the number of distinct elements appearing in this process is given as a(n). Note that it's conjectured that a cycle will be found at some point. Conjecture: The cycle part of each sequence generated by the recursion is one of (4), (5, 6), or (6, 5). Confirmed through 1 millionth term. The conjecture is true. Proof: The conjecture holds for n <= 6. Suppose n >= 7 and the conjecture holds for lower values of n. If n is composite, then A063655(n) <= n/2+2. If n is prime, then A063655(n) = n+1 is even and A063655(A063655(n)) <= (n+1)/2+2. In both cases, n reaches a lower number and the conjecture holds for n. - _Jason Yuen_, Mar 30 2024

name: a(n) is the smallest k such that 2^(2^n+1)-1 + 2^k is prime, or -1 if no such k exists.
text: Conjecture: if n > 0, then 2^(2^n+1)-1 + 2^k is not prime for every k < 2^n. This conjecture seems provable, because it is not too strong for large n > 6. If, for n > 6, a(n) does not exist, then 2^(2^n+1)-1 + 2^k is composite for every natural k. Thus, by the dual Sierpinski conjecture, for n > 6, 2^(2^n+1)-1 is a Sierpinski number, i.e., if n > 6, then (2^(2^n+1)-1)2^k+1 is composite for every natural k. For example, the Mersenne number 2^(2^8+1)-1 may be a dual Sierpinski number. Similarly, if for n > 5, |2^(2^n-1)-1 - 2^m| is not prime for every m > 0, then by the dual Riesel conjecture, 2^(2^n-1)-1 is a Riesel number, i.e., if n > 5, then (2^(2^n-1)-1)2^m-1 is composite for every integer m > 0. For example, the double Mersenne prime 2^(2^7-1)-1 may be a dual Riesel number. By Crocker's theorem; if n > 2, then positive 2^(2^n-1)-1 - 2^m are composite. Let b(n) be the smallest k such that 2^k - (2^(2^n-1)-1) is prime, for n >= 0: {1, 2, 39, 47, 447, 191, ?}. a(7) > 65000, a(8) thru a(12) > 25000, if they exist. - _Robert G. Wilson v_, Jan 22 2024

text: Conjecture: asymptotic mean is 4/9: One third of the primorial base representations (A049345 from which the intermediate value x = A276086(n) is built from) have "2" as their second rightmost digit (out of 0, 1, 2). That 2 is converted by A276086 to 3^2, so as x is a multiple of nine, it is guaranteed that x' [= A003415(x)] gives a multiple of three. If the second rightmost digit is "1", then x = A276086(n) is a multiple of 3 (but not of 9), and its arithmetic derivative, x' = 3*(x/3)' + (x/3), certainly is not a multiple of 3. This leaves the case where the second rightmost digit is "0", and conjecturing now in this case that the modulo 3 remainders are eventually evenly distributed for x' (see A359430 and A373256), at least among the number of the form A048103, it gives in this case 1/3 * 1/3 = 1/9 probability that x' is a multiple of 3, so the total probability would be 1/3 + 0 + 1/9 = 4/9. Note that Sum_{i=1..10^n} a(i), for n = 1..8 gives: 3, 43, 443, 4443, 44443, 444443, 4444444, 44444444, so empirically the value 4/9 seems very sharp. - revised Jun 18 2024.

Presuming his conjecture, the limit would equal kappa, while Mallows estimated it to be "approximately ... 0.277", see A011784. name: Decimal expansion of Mallows's constant or stribolic constant kappa (of order 1).
text: Set kappa_n := A369990(n) / A369991(n) and theta_n := (kappa_n-kappa_{n+1}) / (kappa_{n-1}-kappa_n). Under the hypothesis that theta_{2m} < theta_{2m+2} < theta_{2*m+3} < theta_{2*m+1} for m=1,2,... (verified for all values known so far), we would obtain 0.27887706136895087 < kappa_{21}' < kappa < kappa_{22}' < 0.27887706136898083, which is sharper than formula (3) below. Here, the transformed sequence (kappa_n') = G(kappa_n) is defined via kappa_n' := (kappa_{n-1}*kappa_{n+1} - kappa_n^2) / (kappa_{n-1} - 2*kappa_n + kappa_{n+1}). (See first arXiv article for a proof of this conjecture-dependent statement.) Feeling even more adventurous, we could apply the transformation G four times and would obtain 0.278877061368975064775 < kappa_{19}'''' < kappa < kappa_{18}'''' < 0.278877061368975064815.
